title: Stacks & Queues
tagline: Two disciplined access patterns — LIFO and FIFO — that power everything from undo history to BFS.

sections.content:
Every powerful abstraction in computer science is, at its core, a **constraint**. A stack and a queue do not add new capability to a plain array — they deliberately take capability away. By forbidding random access and restricting where insertions and deletions can occur, they give you something far more valuable: **predictability**. The order in which items come out is guaranteed by the structure itself, not by the discipline of the programmer.

A **stack** enforces **Last-In First-Out (LIFO)**: you can only add and remove from the same end, called the top. Whatever you put in last is the first thing you get back. A **queue** enforces **First-In First-Out (FIFO)**: items enter at the rear and leave from the front — the classic waiting line. These two access disciplines sound almost trivially simple, and yet they appear at every layer of computing: the JavaScript engine managing function calls, the operating system scheduling processes, the network router buffering packets, the text editor tracking edits you have not yet undone.

In this chapter we will build both structures from scratch, analyse their time complexities carefully, trace through the common implementation traps, and study the canonical algorithms — balanced parentheses checking, BFS graph traversal, and the monotonic deque — that demonstrate why these abstractions are so enduring. We will also visit the deque (double-ended queue), a generalisation that gives O(1) access at both ends, and the two-stack queue trick that is a perennial interview favourite.

By the end you will not only know how to implement stacks and queues; you will know *when* to reach for each, why the naive array-shift queue is a performance trap, and how the discipline of restricted access enables the elegant algorithms built on top of it.

sections.title: A Plate Pile and a Ticket Line
sections.content:
A **stack** is the pile of plates in a cafeteria. The kitchen staff load plates from the top, and you as a diner take from the top — the most recently added plate is always the first one you reach. You never rummage through the middle. If a warm plate was placed five minutes ago and a cold one was placed thirty seconds ago, you get the cold one first. This is LIFO: the last plate in is the first plate out.

Notice that this is not a bad design — it is exactly *correct* for the use case. In the JavaScript engine, when `main()` calls `foo()` which calls `bar()`, the engine needs `bar()` to finish *before* it can resume `foo()`, and `foo()` must finish before `main()` can resume. The call stack enforces this nesting structure automatically and perfectly with LIFO ordering. No other policy would work.

A **queue** is the ticket line at a theme park ride. The fairness guarantee is absolute: no matter how attractive or important you are, the person who arrived first boards first. FIFO. This fairness property is exactly what makes queues right for BFS graph traversal — you explore nodes in the order you discover them, ensuring every node at distance *k* from the source is visited before any node at distance *k + 1*. The OS process scheduler uses queues for the same reason: no process should wait forever because newer processes keep cutting in line.

Both analogies reveal the deeper truth: the access policy is not a limitation, it is the *feature*.

sections.title: The Stack in Detail: LIFO Mechanics
sections.content:
A stack exposes exactly three fundamental operations:

- `push(item)` — place an item on top of the stack
- `pop()` — remove and return the top item
- `peek()` (also called `top`) — read the top item without removing it

All three are **O(1)**. That is the whole point. The constraint that you only touch one end means there is never any shifting, searching, or traversal.

The simplest implementation in JavaScript uses a dynamic array and only ever touches the *end* of it. JavaScript's `Array.prototype.push` appends to the end in O(1) amortised time (occasional buffer doubling), and `Array.prototype.pop` removes the last element in strict O(1). As long as you never use `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, or index into arbitrary positions, you have a correct stack.

The amortised O(1) for `push` deserves a brief explanation. Internally, a JavaScript array is a contiguous block of memory. When that block fills up, the runtime allocates a new block roughly double the size, copies all elements, and discards the old block. This copying takes O(n) time in that moment — but because the capacity doubles each time, the amortised cost per push over any sequence of n pushes is O(1). The total copying work across all resizes is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n/2 + n < 2n, so each element is copied on average fewer than two times.

A critical discipline: **never access the middle**. A stack implemented with an array still *has* index access, but as soon as you use it, you have broken the stack abstraction. In interviews and production code alike, the self-discipline is part of the contract.

sections.title: The Queue in Detail: FIFO Mechanics and the O(n) Trap
sections.content:
A queue exposes two core operations:

- `enqueue(item)` — add an item to the rear
- `dequeue()` — remove and return the item at the front

Both should be **O(1)**. The trap is achieving O(1) dequeue.

**The naive implementation and why it fails**: If you model a queue with a JavaScript array, `enqueue` maps naturally to `Array.push` — O(1), good. But `dequeue` from the front maps to `Array.shift`, which removes index 0 and shifts *every remaining element* one position to the left. For an array of n elements, that is O(n) work per dequeue. For n operations this is O(n²) total — catastrophic for a queue of 100,000 items.

**Solution 1: Linked List**. A singly linked list with both a `head` pointer (front) and a `tail` pointer (rear) gives O(1) for both operations. `enqueue` creates a new node and appends it at the tail. `dequeue` reads the head node's value and advances `head` to the next node. The trick is maintaining the `tail` pointer so enqueue never needs to traverse to find the end.

**Solution 2: Circular Buffer**. For bounded queues where you know the maximum capacity, a fixed-size array with two integer indices — `head` and `tail` — that wrap around modulo the capacity is the most cache-friendly option. This avoids heap allocation of nodes entirely and is what high-performance systems like disruptor queues use under the hood.

**Solution 3: Two-Stack Queue** (covered below). This is the classic interview trick that simulates a queue using two stacks, achieving O(1) amortised dequeue through lazy transfer.

sections.explanation: The Stack uses the array end exclusively — push and pop never touch any other index. The Queue uses a linked list with head and tail pointers so both enqueue and dequeue are O(1). When the last node is dequeued, both head and tail are set to null to prevent memory leaks from a dangling tail reference.

sections.title: Classic Stack Application: Balanced Parentheses
sections.content:
The balanced-parentheses problem is the canonical introductory stack problem, and understanding *why* a stack is the right tool here deepens intuition for all future applications.

Given a string like `({[]})`, determine whether every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the correct nested order. The key insight: whenever you encounter a closing bracket, you need to know *the most recently seen unmatched opening bracket*. That is literally the definition of LIFO — the last thing pushed is the first thing needed.

The algorithm: iterate through each character. If it is an opening bracket (`(`, `{`, `[`), push it. If it is a closing bracket, check the top of the stack. If the stack is empty or the top does not match the expected opener, the string is unbalanced. If it matches, pop and continue. At the end, the stack must be empty (no unmatched openers remain).

Why not a queue? If you tried FIFO, you would match the *earliest* opener against each closer — which would accept `([)]` as balanced (open paren matches first close, open bracket matches second close), even though the nesting is wrong. The LIFO ordering of a stack is what enforces correct nesting.

This same pattern extends to: evaluating arithmetic expressions with precedence, implementing undo/redo, tracking function call frames, and parsing HTML/XML tags — all problems where the most-recently-opened context must be resolved before older contexts.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: isBalanced runs in O(n) — one pass with a stack that holds at most n items. The monotonic stack pattern maintains a stack where elements are always in a specific order (here: decreasing). When a new element violates that order by being larger, we pop everything smaller — each element is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n) total even though there is a nested loop.

sections.title: The Two-Stack Queue: Amortised O(1) Dequeue
sections.content:
The two-stack queue is one of the most elegant tricks in data structures and a perennial interview question. The challenge: implement a queue using only two stacks, achieving O(1) amortised dequeue.

Here is the idea. Maintain two stacks: `inbox` and `outbox`. `enqueue` always pushes onto `inbox`. `dequeue` pops from `outbox` — but if `outbox` is empty, first pour everything from `inbox` into `outbox` by popping `inbox` and pushing each item onto `outbox`. This reversal transforms LIFO order back into FIFO order. If `outbox` is still empty after the pour, the queue is empty.

Why is this O(1) amortised? Each element travels a fixed path: it is pushed onto `inbox` once, popped from `inbox` once, pushed onto `outbox` once, and popped from `outbox` once. Four operations total per element, regardless of how many enqueue and dequeue calls happen. Over n operations, the total work is O(n), meaning O(1) per operation amortised.

The worst-case cost of a single dequeue when `outbox` is empty and `inbox` has k items is O(k) — the pour. But that same pour enables the next k dequeues to be O(1), so the expensive case pays for the cheap cases ahead.

This is a beautiful example of **amortised analysis** — reasoning about cost distributed over a sequence of operations rather than worst-case per operation. The same logic applies to dynamic array resizing.

flowchart TD

  IN --> B["dequeue() called"]
  B --> C{"outbox empty?"}
  C -- "No" --> D["pop outbox\nreturn value"]
  C -- "Yes" --> E["pour inbox\ninto outbox"]

sections.caption: Two-stack queue: enqueue is always O(1). Dequeue is O(1) when outbox has items; the pour from inbox to outbox happens at most once per item over the item's lifetime — O(1) amortised.

sections.title: BFS vs DFS: Queue vs Stack at the Algorithmic Level
sections.content:
The connection between traversal algorithms and data structures is one of the most illuminating in all of computer science: **swap the data structure and you swap the algorithm**.

Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level. Start from a source node, visit all its neighbours (distance 1), then all their unvisited neighbours (distance 2), and so on. The data structure that naturally produces this order is a **queue**: you enqueue unvisited neighbours, and FIFO ordering ensures you finish processing all distance-k nodes before any distance-(k+1) node is dequeued.

Depth-First Search (DFS) goes as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. The data structure is a **stack**: you push unvisited neighbours and LIFO ordering means you immediately dive into the most-recently-discovered branch. The recursive form of DFS uses the *call stack* implicitly; the iterative form uses an explicit stack.

The punchline: take the BFS code, replace `queue.enqueue` / `queue.dequeue` with `stack.push` / `stack.pop`, and you get (iterative) DFS. The graph traversal logic — mark visited, process neighbours — stays identical. Only the access policy of the frontier data structure changes, and that single change completely alters the order in which nodes are discovered.

BFS is the right choice when you want shortest paths in unweighted graphs, or level-by-level processing. DFS is the right choice for topological sort, cycle detection, connected components, and backtracking problems. Knowing which structure drives which algorithm is the foundation for every graph problem in interviews.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The two functions are nearly identical — the only mechanical difference is queue.shift() vs stack.pop(). In production code, replace the BFS array-shift with a proper O(1) linked-list queue. The visited set is crucial for graphs with cycles; without it, both algorithms loop forever. The DFS order depends on the order neighbours are pushed — pushing in reverse order gives left-to-right DFS exploration.

sections.title: The Deque: Generalising Both Structures
sections.content:
A **deque** (pronounced 'deck', short for double-ended queue) supports O(1) insertion and removal at *both* ends. It generalises both the stack (use one end only) and the queue (enqueue at one end, dequeue at the other).

Deques are useful whenever you need both-ends flexibility: browser history with Back and Forward buttons (front = forward stack, back = back stack, or a single deque), the work-stealing scheduler in Go's goroutine runtime (goroutines pushed to the rear of one worker's deque; idle workers steal from the *front* of another's deque, avoiding lock contention at the busy end), and the monotonic deque for sliding-window problems.

**The monotonic deque** is one of the most powerful patterns built on top of a deque. Consider the sliding window maximum problem: given an array and a window of size k, find the maximum element in each window position as the window slides right. A naive approach checks all k elements per position — O(nk) total. The monotonic deque brings this to O(n).

The invariant: maintain a deque of *indices* such that the corresponding values are in **decreasing** order from front to back. When a new element arrives, pop from the rear any index whose value is less than or equal to the new element (those can never be the maximum for any future window). Push the new index at the rear. Pop from the front any index that has slid out of the current window. The front of the deque is always the index of the current window's maximum.

Each index is pushed once and popped at most once — O(n) total. The deque's ability to pop from both ends is what makes this possible; neither a pure stack nor a pure queue can do it.

In Python, `collections.deque` is the reference implementation — a doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks (an 'unrolled linked list') providing amortised O(1) at both ends with excellent cache locality. In JavaScript there is no built-in deque; a doubly linked list with `head` and `tail` pointers is the standard implementation.

sections.title: The Circular Buffer: Cache-Friendly Fixed-Size Queue
sections.content:
When the maximum queue size is known in advance, a **circular buffer** (also called a ring buffer) is the most efficient implementation. It uses a fixed-size array and two integer pointers — `head` and `tail` — that advance modulo the capacity.

`enqueue`: write to `array[tail]`, then `tail = (tail + 1) % capacity`. `dequeue`: read from `array[head]`, then `head = (head + 1) % capacity`. Both are O(1) with no heap allocation, no pointer chasing, and excellent cache locality since the entire buffer sits in a contiguous memory block.

The tricky part is distinguishing a full buffer from an empty one, since both have `head === tail`. Two common solutions: (1) keep an explicit `size` counter, or (2) reserve one slot — the buffer is full when `(tail + 1) % capacity === head`.

Circular buffers are ubiquitous in systems programming: kernel I/O ring buffers, audio processing pipelines, producer-consumer patterns in embedded systems, and the Linux `io_uring` interface for high-performance async I/O. They are also the foundation of **disruptor queues** used in financial trading systems where latency of even a microsecond matters.

For interview purposes, you rarely need to implement a circular buffer from scratch — but recognising *when* it is the right choice (bounded capacity, high throughput, cache matters) demonstrates systems thinking beyond basic data structure knowledge.

**Historical context:** The call stack as a hardware concept dates to the late 1950s. Bauer and Samelson patented the stack principle in Germany in 1957, and Charles Hamblin independently described it in 1957 as well. The LIFO discipline was considered so important it was baked into hardware: the Intel 8086 (1978) had dedicated PUSH and POP instructions for its stack pointer. Queues formalised the work of operations research in the 1950s — Erlang's telephone traffic models from the 1910s are the earliest systematic analysis of FIFO waiting lines in engineering. Both abstractions are thus over 60 years old and show no signs of being superseded.

**Interview traps and insights to know cold:**

- **Never use `array.shift()` for dequeue in timed interviews** — it is O(n) and will TLE on inputs of 10⁵ elements. Use a head-pointer trick (`let head = 0; const val = arr[head++]`) or a proper linked-list queue.
- **The two-stack queue is its own interview question** — know it cold: enqueue always goes to `inbox`; dequeue pops from `outbox`, refilling from `inbox` when empty. Amortised O(1).
- **Stack overflow is a real stack** — infinite recursion causes the call stack (which has a fixed maximum depth) to overflow. Rewriting recursive DFS with an explicit stack eliminates this risk.
- **BFS guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs** — DFS does not. If the problem says 'minimum number of steps', reach for BFS + queue.
- **`n & (n-1) === 0` checks if n is a power of 2** — useful when reasoning about circular buffer capacities, which are often chosen as powers of 2 so the modulo wraps with a bitwise AND (`index & (capacity - 1)`).

items: A **stack** is LIFO — push and pop happen at the same end (the top). All operations are O(1). Use a dynamic array and only touch the end — never shift or unshift.

A **queue** is FIFO — enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front. Use a linked list with a tail pointer (or circular buffer) to keep both operations O(1). Using `array.shift()` for dequeue is O(n) and a common performance trap.
The **two-stack queue** achieves O(1) amortised dequeue by lazily pouring `inbox` into `outbox` — each element is moved at most once over its lifetime.

**BFS uses a queue** (level-order, guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs); **DFS uses a stack** (depth-first, implicit via recursion or explicit). Swapping the data structure swaps the algorithm.
A **deque** provides O(1) at both ends, enabling the **monotonic deque** pattern for sliding-window maximum/minimum in O(n) — a technique that reduces O(nk) problems to linear time.

A **circular buffer** is the most cache-friendly bounded queue — two integer pointers advancing modulo capacity, no heap allocation per element, used in OS I/O buffers and high-performance message queues.

The access-policy constraint is the feature, not a limitation: LIFO enforces correct nesting (call stack, expression parsing), FIFO enforces fairness (BFS, scheduling). Choose the structure whose guarantee matches the problem's requirement.

quiz.question: Which access order does a stack enforce?
options: First-In First-Out (FIFO)
Last-In First-Out (LIFO)
Random access by index
Priority-based order
quiz.explanation: A stack is LIFO — the last item pushed is the first item popped. The JavaScript call stack works exactly this way: the most recently called function is the first to return.

quiz.question: Why is `array.shift()` a poor choice for `dequeue` in a high-performance queue?
options: It removes from the wrong end of the array
It is O(n) because it shifts all remaining elements one position to the left
It returns undefined instead of the removed value
It does not work with non-integer values
quiz.explanation: `shift()` removes index 0 and moves every subsequent element one step left — O(n) work per call. For O(1) dequeue use a linked-list queue, a head-pointer trick, or a circular buffer.

quiz.question: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue as its core frontier data structure?
options: Depth-first search (DFS)
Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm
Breadth-first search (BFS)
Topological sort via DFS
quiz.explanation: BFS enqueues unvisited neighbours and dequeues the next node to process. FIFO ordering guarantees all nodes at distance k from the source are visited before any node at distance k+1 — the defining property of level-order traversal.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of push and pop on a stack implemented with a dynamic array (using the array end)?
options: O(n) for both
O(1) for push, O(n) for pop
O(1) amortised for push, O(1) strict for pop
O(log n) for both
quiz.explanation: `push` is O(1) amortised because occasional buffer doubling is the only costly step, and amortised over n pushes the average is O(1). `pop` removes the last element with no shifting — strictly O(1) always.

quiz.question: In the two-stack queue, when does the 'pour' from inbox to outbox occur?
options: After every enqueue operation to keep order correct
Only when dequeue is called and the outbox is empty
Whenever the inbox has more elements than the outbox
At fixed intervals every k operations
quiz.explanation: The pour from inbox to outbox is lazy — it only happens when a dequeue is requested and the outbox is empty. This amortises the O(k) transfer cost across the following k dequeues, giving O(1) amortised per dequeue overall.

quiz.question: A deque (double-ended queue) is most directly useful for which of the following problems?
options: Finding the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph
Maintaining the maximum element in a sliding window of size k in O(n) total
Sorting an array of integers in O(n log n)
Checking whether a number is prime
quiz.explanation: The monotonic deque pattern solves sliding-window maximum/minimum in O(n) by using both ends: the rear receives new elements (popping smaller ones to maintain decreasing order), and the front discards elements that slide out of the window. Neither a pure stack nor pure queue can do both.

quiz.question: How does the two-stack queue achieve O(1) amortised `dequeue`?
options: Always reverse stack 1 into stack 2 on every enqueue operation
Enqueue onto stack 1; on dequeue, if stack 2 is empty pour all of stack 1 into it, then pop stack 2
Use stack 1 for odd-indexed elements and stack 2 for even-indexed elements
Merge both stacks and re-sort after every dequeue
quiz.explanation: Enqueue always pushes onto inbox (stack 1). Dequeue pops from outbox (stack 2); when outbox is empty, pour all of inbox into outbox — reversing the order gives FIFO. Each element is moved at most once, so amortised cost per dequeue is O(1).

quiz.question: Why is a stack the correct data structure for checking balanced parentheses, rather than a queue?
options: A stack is faster than a queue for string traversal
LIFO order matches the nesting structure — the most recently opened bracket must be closed first
A queue cannot store characters, only integers
Stacks use less memory than queues for this problem
quiz.explanation: Nested brackets require that the innermost open bracket is closed first — exactly LIFO semantics. A FIFO queue would match the earliest opener to each closer, wrongly accepting strings like '([)]' as balanced.

quiz.question: In a linked-list queue with head and tail pointers, what is the purpose of the tail pointer?
options: To allow random access to the middle of the queue
To make dequeue O(1) by avoiding traversal from the head
To make enqueue O(1) by directly appending at the rear without traversal
To detect when the queue is empty
quiz.explanation: Without a tail pointer, enqueue would need to traverse the entire list to find the last node — O(n). The tail pointer gives direct access to the rear, making enqueue O(1). Dequeue is O(1) via the head pointer.

quiz.question: What single mechanical change converts an iterative BFS implementation into an iterative DFS implementation?
options: Change the graph representation from adjacency list to adjacency matrix
Add a visited set to track explored nodes
Replace the queue (FIFO dequeue) with a stack (LIFO pop)
Process neighbours in reverse alphabetical order
quiz.explanation: BFS and iterative DFS are structurally identical — mark visited, push/enqueue neighbours, pop/dequeue next node. Replacing the queue with a stack changes the frontier access from FIFO to LIFO, which changes level-order exploration into depth-first exploration. Everything else stays the same.
